articles.summary: Brazil's former President Jair Bolsonaro has been admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) of DF Star hospital in Brasilia after being diagnosed with an
articles.body: Brazil's former President Jair Bolsonaro has been admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) of DF Star hospital in Brasilia after being diagnosed with an acute bowel obstruction. The hospital said on Saturday that the 71-year-old was clinically stable, conscious and breathing without assistance, but there was no forecast for his discharge.Bolsonaro was taken to hospital on Friday after suffering severe abdominal pain. Doctors have started treatment to keep him hydrated, while he has been fitted with a nasogastric tube and placed on fasting with nutritional support.His son Carlos Bolsonaro, in a post on X, said his father was receiving fluids and was being closely monitored by doctors."At the moment, he is stable, conscious, oriented and breathing on his own. No discharge date has been set yet," Carlos wrote in a post on X (translated from Portuguese)."There is hope that his condition will improve. He is being closely monitored and is fighting to get his bowels working again, with his usual grit and focus. No possibility has been ruled out. One day at a time," he added.The latest hospitalisation comes amid Bolsonaro's history of abdominal complications and repeated surgeries following a stabbing during a campaign event in 2018. He has undergone more than nine procedures related to the attack.Following his father's hospitalisation on Friday, Carlos had criticised the conditions under which the former president was being held, alleging that his health had deteriorated because of restricted mobility and what he described as psychological torture."The goal is still to kill Jair Bolsonaro. One way or another," Carlos wrote on X, alleging that his father was not receiving adequate care while in custody.He later said he had been asked to remain at the hospital because no other family members were present, adding that the request had been approved.Bolsonaro governed Brazil from 2019 to 2022 and was sentenced to 27 years in prison last year for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 presidential election to Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.He is serving his sentence under house arrest on medical grounds. His imprisonment followed a trial over allegations that he and his allies attempted to prevent Lula from taking office after the 2022 election.The latest health setback comes weeks after another political blow for the Bolsonaro family. His eldest son, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, lost the October 25 presidential runoff to incumbent Lula, who secured another term in office.Flavio subsequently left Brazil with his family and travelled to the United States via Argentina and Ecuador. articles.title: A Los Angeles diner that had served generations since 1924 shut down in 2025, but has reopened under a nonprofit operator; money earned from meals will now support programmes for people experiencing homelessness
articles.summary: One of the most honourable things someone can do is feed people. Plenty of restaurants perform the noble task and become woven into a city’s fabric.
articles.body: One of the most honourable things someone can do is feed people. Plenty of restaurants perform the noble task and become woven into a city’s fabric. It is not always about the food (although a good plate of pancakes certainly helps). Sometimes, it is about the familiar faces behind the counter, the breakfast you have ordered a hundred times, or the comfort of knowing that a particular place will still be there when you return.For generations of Angelenos, the Original Pantry Cafe was one such place. And after closing its doors in 2025, the century-old diner has rebirthed itself with an even more honourable action.The Original Pantry Cafe reopened in downtown Los Angeles on November 19, 2026, under the management of Hope the Mission, a nonprofit organisation that works to support people experiencing homelessness. The restaurant will continue serving its diner favourites, but now, all profits from the restaurant will support Hope the Mission's work, including providing shelter, meals, housing assistance and other services to people in need. In other words, a meal at the Pantry will now fill the stomach of more than the ones seated.A Los Angeles institution finds its way backThe Original Pantry Cafe first opened in 1924 at the corner of Ninth and Francisco Streets. It later moved to its current location on South Figueroa Street in 1950, where it became a familiar fixture of downtown Los Angeles. Known for its generous breakfast plates, old-fashioned diner interiors and long-standing tradition of staying open around the clock, it welcomed generations of customers through its doors.For years, it was the sort of place where a late-night meal and an early morning breakfast could happen at the same counter. Its menu featured diner staples such as ham and eggs, steak and eggs, pancakes, French toast and sourdough toast. The restaurant also became a piece of the city's history, with former Los Angeles mayor Richard Riordan purchasing it in 1981 and running it until his death in 2023.But in March 2025, after more than a century in business, the Pantry suddenly shut down. Its closure followed a labour dispute between the restaurant's unionised workers and the trust that owned it, which had decided to sell the property. For regular customers, the closure meant saying goodbye to a place that had been part of their routines for decades.Real estate developer Leo Pustilnikov bought the restaurant in September 2025 and later partnered with Hope the Mission to bring it back. The reopening, originally expected much sooner, was delayed after a car crashed into the building, leading to repairs and further permitting work.Now, the familiar dining room is welcoming customers again. The caged cash register, chalk-written specials and classic diner atmosphere have been retained, while the menu has received a few updates. Regulars can still find favourites such as the Pantry Breakfast platter, French toast, coleslaw and sourdough toast. There are also newer additions, including breakfast tacos, a chicken banh mi and meatloaf with a gochujang chilli glaze. The pancakes, meanwhile, are back and made from scratch.A meal that gives backThe biggest change, however, is not on the menu. Hope the Mission will operate the Pantry as a social enterprise, with every bit of profit going towards its work supporting people experiencing homelessness across Los Angeles.The organisation runs shelters and programmes that provide food, housing support, recovery services and assistance to people working towards more stable lives. It hopes the restaurant can generate nearly $50,000 a month to support these efforts. Rather than relying solely on donations, the idea is to turn a much-loved neighbourhood restaurant into a sustainable source of funding for its charitable work.And importantly, the Pantry is still a restaurant. Customers will come in for breakfast, lunch or dinner, pay for their meals and enjoy the same familiar experience, with the profits helping fund services elsewhere in the city.The reopening also brings back some of the people who helped make the Pantry what it was. Longtime employees are returning under a new agreement with UNITE HERE Local 11, the union representing the restaurant's workers. Their return is an important part of restoring the restaurant's identity, because a place is often remembered just as much for the people who serve you as for what arrives on your plate.There are a few things that have not quite returned yet. The Pantry is no longer open 24 hours a day, operating from 7 am to 9 pm Sunday to Thursday and until 11 pm on Fridays and Saturdays. Its new management has said it hopes to gradually bring back round-the-clock service as business grows.For now, though, the doors are open again. And there is something rather fitting about a restaurant that has spent more than 100 years bringing people together around a table finding a new way to serve its community. The Original Pantry Cafe is still dishing out breakfast, still making room for familiar faces and still giving Los Angeles a reason to pull up a chair. Only now, every meal comes with the promise of helping someone else find a little more stability.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Who is BrycexD? Inside the New Zealand streamer’s 40-hour attempt to finish GTA 6 first
articles.summary: BrycexD, a Twitch streamer based in New Zealand, has attracted attention after claiming to be the first person in the world to complete the official
articles.body: BrycexD, a Twitch streamer based in New Zealand, has attracted attention after claiming to be the first person in the world to complete the official release version of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6). He revealed that he reached the game’s ending in 39 hours, 38 minutes and 22 seconds after staying awake for more than 50 hours. However, his claim of holding the first GTA 6 speedrun world record has not been officially verified. His achievement also came with an unusual detail: he admitted that he had skipped the entire story and had no idea what happened in the game.Who is BrycexD? How the New Zealand Twitch streamer claimed to finish GTA 6 firstBrycexD is a Twitch streamer who went live with a challenge to complete GTA 6 before anyone else. Being based in New Zealand also gave him an early opportunity to start playing because the game became available there ahead of several other regions.On November 20, 2026, he took to X to announce that he had reached the end of the official game. He also shared his completion time and claimed that his livestream had reached a combined peak audience of 14,000 viewers.In his announcement, BrycexD wrote:“WE DID IT!!! I’m the very first person in the world to beat the official release version of Grand Theft Auto 6! I also now hold the speedrun world record, as I stayed up for 50+ hours and took no breaks. 14,000 Combined CCV Peak, 6,126 Subs,12.2K Total, DCTY Verifier.”The streamer claimed that he had stayed awake for more than 50 hours to complete the challenge. His reported game completion time, however, was just under 40 hours. He also shared evidence showing that he had reached the end credits.But completing the game so quickly did not mean he had experienced its full story. After getting some rest, BrycexD returned to X with another update that revealed what he had missed during the marathon.He wrote:“14 hours of sleep later and I’m still tired from this. Time to actually play the game since I skipped the entire story lmao. I actually have no idea what happens in this game.”His admission made it clear that his main aim during the challenge was to reach the ending as quickly as possible, rather than follow the story and experience everything the game had to offer.Has BrycexD’s GTA 6 world record been officially verified?Despite his announcement, BrycexD’s claim of becoming the first person worldwide to complete GTA 6 has not been independently confirmed. Reaching the end credits provides evidence that he finished the game, but it does not establish that nobody else completed it before him.GamesRadar+ also pointed out that Speedrun.com’s GTA 6 leaderboards were not due to open for another 41 and a half days at the time of its November 20 report. This means there was no official leaderboard system in place to review and recognise his claimed record.There is also a difference between being the first publicly known streamer to reach the ending and being the first person in the world to do so. Other players could have completed the main story without livestreaming their attempts or sharing recordings online. Someone could also have finished it in less time.For now, BrycexD’s 39-hour, 38-minute and 22-second run remains his reported achievement rather than an officially recognised world record.Following the response to his announcement, the streamer also returned to X to thank the people who watched and supported his challenge. He admitted that he had expected a much smaller audience and was surprised by how many people joined his livestream.He wrote:“Not trying to milk the cow dry here but I need to say it one last time. THANK YOU to everyone who showed up for my world’s first GTA 6 completion stream. I thought I’d only see 10-20 people show up. Love all of you so much, man. Couldn’t have been better.”His message reflected how much the response meant to him, even as questions remained about the world-first claim.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.body: The Ohio State Buckeyes have one of the most expensive rosters in college football, but on Saturday, that didn't matter a lick. Nebraska rode a little home cooking and some fourth quarter magic to secure one of its biggest wins in the last decade, taking down the Buckeyes 31-28. Couple that with relatively mistake-free football (Nebraska was plus-two in the turnover battle), and you get what is perhaps head coach Matt Rhule's signature win in his fourth year in Lincoln. If the Huskers can win next week in Iowa City, they will have completed the most successful season since Mike Riley won nine games in 2016. articles.title: Lock of former US President George Washington's hair sells for $4,000
articles.summary: The hair was given as a sign of friendship shortly before Washington's death in 1799, according to a descendent of its former owner.
articles.body:
A framed lock of hair from America's first president, George Washington, has been sold at auction for $4,000 (£3,058).

The hair once belonged to John Gadsby, who entertained Washington in 1799 just before the latter's death the same year, and was later obtained by a collector called John K Lattimer from a descendent of Gadsby's, according to Richmond Auctions, which sold the item.

Saturday's sale is not the most expensive for Washington hair at auction. Three strands thought to have been removed from him close to or after his death stored in a locket sold for nearly $40,000 in 2021.

Gadsby, a resident of what in 1799 was the town of Alexandria in Virginia, entertained Washington for dinner shortly before his death later that year, according to a testament given in 1928 by Gadsby's granddaughter, Julia Ten Eyck McBlair, and which was posted on the Richmond Auctions website.

McBlair stated that her grandfather came into possession of Washington's hair "in view of the friendship and association with his last days" and had it framed and hung "under General Washington's portrait in our home in Washington City, there I have seen it all my life".

Gadsby hosted Washington's two birthday celebrations in 1798 and 1799, Richmond Auctions states.

Washington led American forces to victory against the British in the War of Independence and helped draft the US Constitution before becoming the country's first president in 1788. He stepped down in 1797 after serving two terms.

Several locks of Washington's hair have been preserved, including at least 50 examples that are in a collection at his former residence, Mount Vernon, which is now a museum.

"Public displays of hair from friends or loved ones peaked in the 19th century, but had long been popular among affluent families like the Washingtons," a blog on the Mount Vernon website states.

As well as lockets of his hair, other items associated with Washington have also done well at auction.

In July, a signed letter by Washington from 1776, in which he asks for soldiers for the Continental Army to fight the British, sold for $109,800.

articles.summary: For Audrey and Wills W., a lottery ticket bought as a Mother's Day gift turned into a $70 million windfall, changing the plans they had made for their
articles.body: For Audrey and Wills W., a lottery ticket bought as a Mother's Day gift turned into a $70 million windfall, changing the plans they had made for their retirement. The Brampton couple, who moved to Canada from Jamaica several decades ago in search of a better life, had spent years working, saving and living within their means. Neither had expected a single ticket to bring such a dramatic change to their circumstances. There was an unexpected twist, though. Before they had even confirmed the result themselves, their daughter had begun to suspect that the enormous Lotto Max prize might have gone to her parents.Mother's Day lottery gift turns into a $70 million jackpotThe winning ticket came from a gesture by Wills, who had bought Audrey a Lotto Max quick pick for Mother's Day. It was entered on the 08 May 2026 draw, which carried a jackpot of $70 million. The ticket was purchased at Canco One Stop Gas Station on Steeles Avenue in Brampton, according to the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation (OLG).Audrey eventually checked the numbers through the OLG app. What appeared on her phone initially left her uncertain about the amount she was seeing. She called Wills over to look at the screen, asking whether the figure was really $70. He realised that she had overlooked the additional zeros. Once the full amount became clear, the couple had to take a moment to process what had happened.Audrey described her reaction as one of disbelief, followed by an outburst of excitement. She began jumping on the bed before dropping to her knees, overwhelmed by the realisation that they had won the entire jackpot.For Wills, the excitement took a slightly different form. He said he could feel the anticipation running through his body, even though he appeared composed from the outside. The result had taken them by surprise, but their daughter seemed to have reached the conclusion earlier.Daughter says ‘I knew it!’ after parents reveal their $70 million lottery winNews that a winning Lotto Max ticket had been sold in Brampton had already begun circulating before Audrey and Wills shared their news with their daughter. Having heard about the location of the winning ticket, she apparently suspected that her parents might be the people behind the extraordinary win.When the couple eventually told her, she did not appear particularly surprised. Instead, she smiled and told them that she had known it. Audrey recalled the exchange in her account to OLG, suggesting that her daughter's suspicion had preceded the family's official confirmation of the result. The coincidence added an unusual detail to a story that had begun with an ordinary holiday gift.Couple who built their lives from scratch plan carefully after lottery windfallThe couple's story stretches back several decades, to their move from Jamaica to Canada. They arrived with very little, hoping to establish a better life in their new country. Over the years, they worked towards financial stability and developed habits centred on saving rather than spending beyond their means.Audrey spoke about their background while explaining why they intended to approach the lottery money carefully. articles.title: Immigration officers make arrests at Seattle airport in 'distressing' scene, delaying flight
articles.summary: Masked immigration officers detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, causing what the airline called...
articles.body:
Masked immigration officers detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, causing what the airline called a "distressing" scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight.

Video of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as a woman screams that her daughter is being taken and she has a work permit.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who "overstayed his visa in violation of our nation's laws."

During the confrontation, another passenger "hurled hot coffee on the officers," the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

Online flight data showed that Alaska flight 1306, which had been scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m., was delayed.

Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

"We are concerned by this morning's law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306," the airline said. "We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests."

It added that the airline is committed to "treating every guest with dignity and respect."

The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The video showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases look on.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns "directly with the appropriate authorities."

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would "engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred."

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE's tactics were "deeply un-American" and called for the agency's abolition.

"The video is horrific and it is chilling," Ferguson said at an afternoon news conference with labor leaders and local elected officials. "We need a system of immigration enforcement and border security that is effective, ethical and humane. And ICE is not it. It is beyond reform."

Ferguson also said he was looking into how ICE agents accessed the jet bridge and he believes they violated a state law he signed in March limiting facial coverings on law enforcement officers.

April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, representing over 600,000 workers, said union members were aboard the flight. She said the action disrupted travel during one of the busiest times and only days after flights were grounded nationwide due to a communications problem. "Airport workers are already managing extraordinary stress, passengers are already anxious and instead of restoring calm and confidence, federal agents introduced more fear and more chaos," she said.

articles.title: Dior: Could Paul Mescal's GAA shorts craze be making its way to the catwalk?
articles.summary: A casting call for sportsmen in Dublin has sparked speculation that Northern Irish designer Jonathan Anderson could be bringing an unexpected influence to his first Dior show in Ireland.
articles.body:
A casting call for sportsmen in Dublin has sparked speculation that Northern Irish designer Jonathan Anderson could be bringing an unexpected influence to his first Dior show in Ireland.

The rumours began after Dublin modelling agency Not Another Intl advertised for sports stars - particularly Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA) players - to take part in a show on 4 December.

The date is significant as it coincides with Dior's presentation of its 2027 autumn/winter collection at Trinity College Dublin.

Although the identity of the agency's client has not been revealed, fashion fans have been quick to speculate that Anderson, Dior's creative director, could be keen to bring a distinctly Irish touch to the catwalk.

The show will mark the designer's first runway presentation on the island of his birth - and Dior's first catwalk show in Ireland too.

The speculation comes amid a wider revival of interest in Irish sporting style, with Gaelic games shorts becoming an unlikely fashion statement in recent years.

The distinctive sportswear, made by Irish brand O'Neill's, received international attention after actor Paul Mescal wore a pair while playing Connell Waldron in the television adaptation of Normal People.

Mescal, from County Kildare, played rugby and hurling until he was about 13 before going on to become an under-21 Gaelic footballer for the county.

The 30-year-old has since been photographed wearing the shorts on several occasions, including around London, at the Coachella festival and in GQ magazine.

Their popularity has helped turn a familiar piece of Irish sportswear into an internationally recognised style item.

An Instagram post appearing to be from the agency Not Another Intl said its client was searching for sports players of all ethnicities who are available between the end of November and 5 December.

The social media advert states that no modelling experience is required, with applicants needing to be male, aged between 17 and 25 and at least 6ft 1in (1.8m) tall.

The Irish Times reported that a model agent for the agency confirmed that the casting call was legitimate but did not disclose the client's identity.

Dior is expected to fly its own models to Dublin for the presentation.

It is understood that Not Another Intl is not involved in the brand's Trinity College production, and it remains unclear what role the models recruited through the casting call will play.

Emily O'Donnell, a fashion broadcaster and stylist, says that if it turns out to be genuine it is "very exciting" and would be a "great move" for Anderson.

"The best shows in fashion are always ones with diversity," she says.

"If you're doing it on home turf, it's definitely great to have a few Irish lads storming down the catwalk."

O'Donnell says that if the casting call is unrelated to Dior it is "the best publicity stunt ever".

"I don't have any inside information on any other shows that are taking place around there in Ireland so it's definitely very coincidental, I'll say that.

"There's definitely a lot of chat about it, everybody's wondering what's happening and I think it's a bit of excitement as well for people."

O'Donnell says the renewed interest in Irish fashion and heritage was something to celebrate.

Following on from the O'Neill's shorts craze, O'Donnell thinks "it's brilliant that we're now proudly celebrating all our own stuff, which I love".

Anderson bringing Dior to Ireland could also inspire a new generation of designers, according to O'Donnell.

She believes the show offers local creatives an opportunity to see what is possible for Irish fashion on the international stage.

"It's setting the creative fires alight. It's giving people that real growth for all things Irish as well.

"The way he's incorporated Guinness, the shamrocks [into his designs], all of the things that I suppose are ironically Irish into his designs has actually led to a surge in people trying to source vintage Irish pieces.

"It's great for the whole of Ireland, not just from a design point of view but also for a tourism point of view because the spotlight is now on our gorgeous country and all it has to offer."

It would not be the first time Anderson has woven uniquely Irish culture into his designs.

The fashion house's Cruise 2027 runway show featured a shirt printed with the phrase "Says I, to myself, says I", sparking widespread comparison to Uncle Colm who often began meandering stories in this way in the TV show Derry Girls.

Sport and fashion have also crossed paths before in Ireland, with former Kerry Gaelic footballer Paul Galvin launching his own clothing line and Irish League football manager and former player David Jeffrey getting into modelling.

But it is the prospect of GAA players appearing alongside the world's leading fashion talent that has captured imaginations ahead of the December show.

Born in Magherafelt, County Londonderry, Anderson is one of the most influential designers in the world .

The 40-year-old is known for his innovative styles and gender-fluid designs, and has created some iconic and recognisable looks throughout his career.

In 2023, he crafted Rihanna's Super Bowl half-time performance outfit , which she used to announce her pregnancy and Ariana Grande's 2024 Met Gala gown.

Anderson trained at the London College of Fashion before beginning his career in Prada's marketing department.

He launched his own label JW Anderson in 2008 and was appointed creative director of Spanish luxury fashion house Loewe in 2013.

He became the first designer to lead both divisions at the French fashion house, which was founded in Paris by Christian Dior in 1946.

articles.title: MrBeast's legal battle takes new turn as former employee agrees to forensic inspection over stolen files
articles.summary: MrBeast's business empire has reached a legal agreement that brings a troubling workplace dispute closer to resolution.
articles.body: MrBeast's business empire has reached a legal agreement that brings a troubling workplace dispute closer to resolution. The YouTube star's company accused a former senior employee of taking thousands of confidential files and allegedly placing hidden cameras inside its offices. The allegations raised serious questions about the security of one of the internet's biggest creator-led businesses. Now, both sides have agreed on a settlement process, but the case is not entirely over. The former employee must first undergo a detailed inspection of his personal devices and accounts.MrBeast settles lawsuit over alleged stolen company filesMrBeast's media company, which operates under YouTube creator Jimmy Donaldson's business empire, reached an agreement with former development director Leroy Nabors on November 20. Lawyers for both parties informed the court that they had settled the dispute.However, the agreement comes with a key condition. Nabors must allow a forensic examination of his devices and online accounts to establish whether confidential company information remains in his possession or has been shared elsewhere.The court filing outlined what would happen next. “Upon satisfactory completion of the Protocol, Beast will voluntarily dismiss this action,” the document stated. The dismissal would be “without prejudice,” allowing the company to bring the lawsuit again if necessary.The dispute began after Nabors, who joined the business as an IT contractor in 2023 before moving into a leadership role, allegedly downloaded thousands of internal documents when he learned that his employment was ending.According to the complaint, the files included financial records, information about investors and business transactions, and confidential plans behind MrBeast's popular video productions. The company also alleged that Nabors wiped his laptop after downloading the material.When questioned, he reportedly described the transfer as a routine “backup” carried out during his regular work. He also allegedly refused to return the documents.Hidden cameras allegations raise security concerns at MrBeast's companyThe allegations went beyond missing documents. During its internal investigation, MrBeast's company claimed it discovered several hidden cameras across its office premises.Investigators also reportedly found a device connected to company servers that contained software capable of allowing remote access and control of its network. The company suspected Nabors was responsible for installing the equipment.The complaint further stated that Nabors' daughter had worked as a contractor managing the company's IT network and had access to the camera feeds. However, these remain allegations made in the lawsuit, not findings established by a court.MrBeast's company accused Nabors of misappropriating trade secrets and breaching his contract, among other claims, while seeking unspecified damages.The case also offered a rare look inside Donaldson's growing media operation. Its development department handles everything from video production to fundraising and political advocacy. articles.title: Job ghosting: What applicants can do if employers do not respond
articles.summary: People say they often hear nothing back after applying for jobs. But could employers be forced to respond to every applicant?
articles.body:
Have you ever applied for a job or attended an interview, only to hear absolutely nothing back from the employer?

So-called "job ghosting" has become a big problem for jobseekers in the UK, leaving them "demoralised", denting their confidence and undermining their hopes of finding work.

It's an issue that was mentioned in former minister Alan Milburn's major review into young people who are not in employment, education or training - those dubbed as Neets - this week.

Among his recommendations - aimed at reducing the proportion of Neets from 13% to about 5% by 2036 - Milburn proposed that large employers should give all unsuccessful job applicants under 25 "meaningful feedback".

The report's proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to suit their own systems.

But is feedback for all applicants realistic, given the vast number of applications these firms receive? And what can people do to improve their chances in such a tough job market?

Yugraj Samrai, 23, from Coventry is currently unemployed and says he has submitted hundreds of job applications since he graduated from his marketing degree in July.

But 30 to 40% of the time he hears nothing back at all, which can make him "feel like a statistic, not a person".

He tells the BBC: "I understand there are very few graduate jobs available, but at least give me a response to say whether I'll progress onto the next stage or not.

"I've spent all that time and energy submitting my application but got nothing in return."

Ffion Johns, from Llanelli, has been unemployed since June and did not get an interview until September after submitting 70 applications.

The 24-year-old says her biggest challenge throughout the job-hunting process has been not getting feedback about why she didn't get the job, so she knows what to fix next time.

She says she has also been ghosted after interviews several times.

"With most of these roles I'm not getting a rejection. I'm just not hearing anything, which can be quite frustrating," she says.

Research by head-hunting firm Robert Walters last year found 86% of UK job hunters said their applications had been ignored, with no response at all from the hiring organisation.

The Milburn report says this "wall of silence" is especially hard on young people as it gives them "nothing to learn from". It adds that "time and emotional investment" goes into their applications.

"It can really take hours and hours, so it just feels even worse to not even have that be recognised," says Jessica Anderson, a 21-year-old, from Swindon.

Employers say they are being flooded with job applications in a very competitive jobs market and it can be hard to respond to all of them.

And AI is adding to the problem, enabling applicants to submit large numbers of applications in the hope of improving their chances.

But Meg Burton, a career coach based in Leeds, says firms should at the very least inform job applicants when they are unsuccessful and that AI could help achieve this.

Candidates should also be given proper feedback if they reach the interview stage, she says.

"It doesn't have to be hugely detailed, it's just some pointers on why they were unsuccessful and what they can learn from that experience going forward," she says.

The government could choose to adopt the Milburn proposals and crack down on job ghosting.

But it raises another question: if candidates began receiving significantly more rejections than before, could this itself have a demoralising effect?

Ellie McCrone, 20, from Northampton understands the concern but thinks hearing back and getting constructive feedback where possible is always best.

"If you are applying for hundreds of jobs and never getting anything, I think something is going wrong... You can't fix something unless you know what the problem is."

There are things applicants can do to improve their chances and avoid ghosting, such as tailoring their CV to each job and not submitting "hundreds and hundreds of applications" that all look the same, Burton adds.

Candidates should also never take being ghosted personally, she adds.

"Not hearing back doesn't mean you aren't a great candidate. Put it down to experience and move on."

articles.title: From pit-stops to go-to destinations: The transformation of service stations
articles.summary: Once a quick pause on a long trip, service stations are becoming destinations in their own right.
articles.body:
Service stations have been a fixture on the nation's motorway network for more than six decades, but while they may once have been just a place to go when needing a break on a long drive, could it be that these roadside retreats have now evolved into destinations in their own right?

Next to the motorway near Rotherham, where traffic seems to be forever thundering by, is a covered square, surrounded by what at first appears to be sandy-coloured stone buildings - and there is a general air of calm.

But this is not one of many pretty rural villages that dot the Yorkshire countryside - this is actually the service station which was recently named in survey as the UK's favourite.

While it is only mid-morning, the Welcome Break site's concourse is already bustling.

A father, juggling a tray of coffee and his small child, heads straight upstairs to the soft play area.

Outside the main building, there is a doggy exercise area and even a gym for HGV drivers.

In the recent Transport Focus survey, 123 service stations were ranked, but it was this place, which opened in January 2025, which came top with a 99% satisfaction rating. A number of operators opted out of taking part in the watchdog's annual review, although 37,000 visitors shared their views.

It is a long way from when drivers pulling in for a refuel and refresh may have picked their stop by a simple little symbol on a physical map, with no idea what the site may look like.

But these days, the topic of service stations is tagged thousands of times on TikTok, with some videos of Welcome Break Rotherham racking up over 500,000 views.

According to content creator Richard Cross, social media is a "major player" in raising the profile of today's service stations.

Dubbed "The Services King", the 28-year-old motoring enthusiast says he has noticed "a shift in the offers we've got on motorway service areas" since an increase in social media coverage.

"Everybody's had to improve and up their game to cater for those new audiences," he says.

"I think it taught a lot of people that they want more value for their money, but they also want a better quality product as a result of that."

Cross says his own interest in service stations was inspired by his childhood travels with his lorry driver father.

He has since stopped at all the UK's official motorway service stations, and regularly documents his visits online.

"There's always a new story to tell within motorway services," he explains.

"Whether that be from recent investment from an operator, or unearthing new historical facts and information that we've not found before."

Stations sometimes become synonymous with a particular product or offering - think Tebay's Cumberland sausage rolls, or Gloucester's farm shop produce .

Newer sites in particular can cater to new customer expectations, Cross says.

One of the UK's first motorway service stations was Watford Gap in Northhamptonshire , which opened in 1959, the same day as Newport Pagnell Services.

Owned by RoadChef, this year it was ranked last in the Transport Focus survey - but still achieved a satisfaction rating of 86%.

"We are seeing big, airy, open buildings now, letting all that natural light in, and I think we'll continue to see that as they evolve over time," Cross explains.

"Beforehand, they were catering for a different level of traffic back then, and offering a different set-up as well.

"Those buildings are now starting to become just a little bit too compact for what modern day expectations are."

Like Cross, retail expert Jonathan De Mello, believes the function of motorway service stations is evolving to keep up with a diverse array of demands.

"You can do a lot more in service stations than you could in the past," he explains.

"It was just a pit-stop on the way to somewhere else. Now it's almost trying to increase dwell times through the presence of a mix of operators [to] facilitate that."

De Mello suggests one reason for this could be due to residential housing developments being built further outside cities, with less access to retail offerings.

Service stations then act as "hubs for local convenience", he says.

"These service stations become quite good ports of call for certain items, like groceries or health and beauty products.

"Traditional high street traders are now at service stations, and that makes the destinations for people that live in the area, as well as people passing through."

Welcome Break's CEO John Diviney agrees that although the primary function of a service station is still to provide a place to rest and refuel, "people definitely look for more than just an in and out".

"I think people always want the best of everything they can get whenever they do anything, and people's expectations over the years continue to rise," he says.

Service station providers have to consider multiple factors to match that demand, Diviney explains, such as "the brands that we offer [and] that wi-fi is there if they want to do work emails while the car is charging on site".

"And we need to make all that available to them," he adds.

A little further along the M1, located outside Leeds, is Skelton Lake services.

The site, run by Extra, backs onto Skelton Lake Country Park, a popular dog-walking spot.

Tim and Marie, travelling with their four terriers back to Nottinghamshire from North Yorkshire, say they regularly choose to pause here when travelling.

"It's a really nice location to stop off," Marie explains.

"On the way up, we were directed off the motorway so we we had to stop at another one and they're definitely not as dog friendly.

"This has got this beautiful grassy area so we can walk."

If she lived locally, it would be "handy to pop in for some of the outlets they've got", she adds.

Sitting on a bench overlooking the lake, Wayne and dachshund Fritz are heading home after a holiday in Whitby.

"We come here every single time we pass," he says.

"I've done it since it opened because it's probably the best service station for dog walking. As soon as we realised it has lakes at the back, we don't go anywhere else."

Wayne says he hopes more service stations will develop areas designed for dogs, and their owners, to stretch their legs.

"There's a lot more dog ownership now. If you're walking around a car park, it can actually be quite dangerous with all the cars," he says.

Looking to the future, more electric vehicles (EVs) on the road could also drive the trend of service stations transforming into leisure destinations, De Mello says.

According to government data, there are more than two million EVs registered on UK roads, with one in four new cars sold now being fully electric models.

"People are staying longer because, rather than just filling up the tank with petrol and going on your way, you're sitting there while your car charges," De Mello explains.

"So having a service station that has more facilities naturally means there are going to be more opportunities to spend."

However, Cross says he is "still to be convinced" of the long-term influence an increase in EV vehicle ownership will have on the service station industry.

He points out that as technology improves, charging times could drop, so operators may not want to "put all their eggs in one basket".

Cross predicts the trend for "offline" sites, located between junctions rather than directly off the motorway, could continue.

"They are more accessible to locals as well as passing traffic, and I think we're going to continue to see that as we get new motorway services because it captures a new market," he says.

Cross says his own content has been through an evolution in itself, although his love for the UK's service station scene remains as strong as ever.

"Before, I was just turning up to sites, taking a couple of photographs and then disappearing.

"Now it's more about taking time to spend that extra couple of hours on a motorway service area or a petrol forecourt."

He says it is all about "getting to know the staff that work there, the operators that operate those locations and hearing their perspective of how the industry works and how their specific site plays into that industry".

"For me, it's such a fascinating perspective to kind of understand and hear," he adds.

articles.title: Parents urged to spot online stalking warning signs as cases rise
articles.summary: From fake profiles to unwanted contact, specialists explain the signs parents should take seriously.
articles.body:
Parents are being urged to recognise the signs of online stalking, amid concerns technology is making it easier than ever for perpetrators to monitor and repeatedly contact young people.

Experts say persistent unwanted contact, attempts to bypass blocks by creating new accounts and efforts to track someone's online activity can all be early indicators of stalking behaviour.

Their advice follows the case of a Wiltshire teenager who became "obsessed" with a girl after a five-day relationship, monitoring her online activity and creating fake social media accounts after she blocked him before later attacking her with a knife.

It also comes as stalking offences have risen across Avon and Somerset, with police recording 1,348 offences last year, up from 954 two years earlier.

In response to the increase, officers are receiving additional training to help identify stalking behaviour, patterns of control and links to other offences.

Gloucester Crown Court heard the 14-year-old boy had become "obsessed" with the girl after she ended their relationship.

The victim's mother told the BBC: "She had no idea that he was logging when she was online, who she was speaking to, what she was saying.

"There were diaries found in his house [detailing her online activity]. It makes me feel sick."

The court heard the boy created numerous fake social media accounts to contact the victim after she blocked him, before later attacking her with a 6in knife.

He admitted wounding with intent, inflicting grievous bodily harm and possession of a bladed article in a public place, but avoided a custodial sentence .

"This is something you watch happen to other people and you're horrified by it. But now this is my life, and that happened to my child," the victim's mother added.

Police guidance describes stalking as repeated, unwanted behaviour that is fixated or obsessive and affects a person's daily life.

While many people associate stalking with being followed in public, experts say it can increasingly take place online through social media platforms, messaging apps and gaming services.

Researchers have suggested tools including GPS trackers , social media, home surveillance systems and smartphone apps may be contributing to a wider rise in stalking cases, making it easier for perpetrators to monitor victims remotely.

Trowbridge-based stalking charity FearFree said concerns should not be dismissed, even when behaviours appear minor at first.

"We know that sometimes - particularly when the behaviour first starts - it can be hard to recognise the risk it might pose, but it is important to not dismiss your concerns," a spokesperson said.

"Evidence shows us that stalking is a high risk behaviour, which can lead to serious violence."

Research by the University of Gloucestershire and the Suzy Lamplugh Trust found 94% of murders examined featured prior stalking behaviour.

Campaigners say concerns about recognising stalking behaviours early have been raised nationally for years, with high-profile cases highlighting the dangers of warning signs being overlooked.

Police say stalking is often characterised by a pattern of unwanted behaviour rather than a single incident.

Warning signs can include somebody continuing to send messages after being asked to stop, creating new accounts after being blocked, or keeping track of when a person is online and who they are speaking to.

Other behaviours can include attempting to infiltrate friendship groups, turning up unexpectedly at places a person regularly visits, sending unwanted gifts or communications, or spreading rumours about them.

In some cases, stalkers may also try to gain access to email, social media or other online accounts to monitor a victim's activity.

What should parents do if they are worried?

If stalking is carried out online, victims are encouraged to make social media accounts private, avoid publicly sharing their location - unless it is with a trusted friend or family member - and protect their devices and accounts with strong passwords.

Although blocking a stalker may seem the obvious response, Gloucestershire-based charity the Hollie Gazzard Trust warns that obsessed perpetrators may be "more likely to physically come round and find you".

Instead, Gloucestershire Constabulary advises victims to keep contact with the stalker to a minimum.

"Blocking can result in a stalker changing their behaviour, which in turn escalates the risk of violence," a spokesperson said.

The force says previous messages, posts and records of unwanted contact can provide important evidence about the volume and nature of the behaviour.

"However, we also understand how distressing it can be when you are the victim of this type of behaviour," the force continued.

"We would encourage anyone who is experiencing this to speak to us or a recognised organisation who can help provide advice and support."

When should stalking be reported to police?

Under UK law, stalking and harassment offences generally require two or more related incidents of unwanted behaviour to warrant police intervention.

However, police stress victims do not need evidence before making contact, although information such as dates, times and witness details can help investigators.

Personal safety charity the Suzy Lamplugh Trust offers online resources for tracking and recording stalking behaviours .

"Anything you've got like that can be useful to us, but don't delay reporting to get it," Wiltshire Police advises.

"Your information could help us bring the offender to justice and make sure you, and other people in a similar situation, are kept safe."

What happens after a stalking report is made?

Once a report is made, police will assess whether an offence has been committed, how serious the behaviour is and whether the victim is at immediate risk.

If there are viable lines of enquiry, an investigating officer will usually be assigned and the case may then be referred for further action, including criminal prosecution.

Stalking carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison, and a Stalking Protection Order (SPO) can also be enforced to protect a victim of any age.

The conditions of the order could include prohibiting the stalker from entering certain locations, approaching or contacting the victim, making direct or indirect references to the victim on social media, recording images of the victim, and more.

Breaching an SPO is deemed a criminal offence under the Stalking Protection Act 2019, and could carry a maximum sentence of up to five years in prison.

If you have been affected by issues of harassment and stalking , information and support is available via the The National Stalking Helpline on 0808 802 0300.

articles.title: Nigeria election 2027: Why are its politicians so old in a young country?
articles.summary: Fewer young people have registered to vote in next year's election than in 2023 - are young people losing faith in democracy?
articles.body:
Abdulhadi Dalhatu is something of a rarity in Nigeria politics.

At 38, he is among the young people seeking elected office in a country where about 80% of the population is under 40.

He hopes his age will stand in his favour as he campaigns for a seat in the state assembly in the northern Kano state in January's general elections.

"Younger people are the majority in this country and should be deciding the future," Dalhatu tells the BBC.

But Nigeria's political history suggests he faces an uphill battle.

Since the return to civilian rule in 1999, Goodluck Jonathan has been the youngest person elected president, taking office at the age of 53.

The current president, Bola Tinubu, is 74 and would be 79 by the end of a second term if he is re-elected in January.

His main challengers are also considerably older. Atiku Abubakar, seeking the presidency for the seventh time, is 79, while Peter Obi is 65.

Of the 18 presidential candidates, only one is under 40 - Moses Olusoji Adebisi, a 35-year-old businessman representing the Democratic Leadership Alliance (DLA).

Although he says he is confident of winning, few Nigerians appear to know much about him and he has not been seen much on the campaign trail.

The contrast is striking in a country with one of the world's youngest populations, where young people have repeatedly demonstrated their ability to shape political debate and mobilise for change.

In the previous election, Obi, then 61, galvanised millions of young Nigerians through a social media-driven movement known as the "Obedients".

His campaign promised a break from the established political order, appealing particularly to young people struggling to find jobs and earn a decent living.

But his failure to win the presidency left many of his supporters disillusioned.

"At the time we were so hopeful, but unfortunately the result wasn't what we wanted, which made many lose hope in the system," former Obedient Nonso Chukwudi tells the BBC.

The movement had built on the momentum of the EndSars protests in 2020, which grew into one of Nigeria's biggest youth-led movement in decades.

Initially sparked by anger over police brutality, the demonstrators developed into a wider call for political reform, accountability and greater youth participation in governance.

But the protests were eventually crushed by the authorities. About 56 were reportedly killed, although officials dispute this figure, while hundreds were arrested and some had their bank accounts frozen.

Both EndSars and the Obedients demonstrated the capacity of young Nigerians to mobile around political causes.

But turning that enthusiasm into sustained electoral participation has proved much harder.

Hajara Musa, 33, is among those who have lost faith in the political system. She has no plans to register or vote in the near future.

"I just feel like things are already determined and I'll just be wasting my time. It is going to be the same people all over again," she tells the BBC.

The electoral register appears to reflect this growing disillusionment.

Although the number of registered voters has increased by 10 million to over 103 million since the last election, enrolment of those under 35 has actually fallen, by about seven million.

Young people now account for just 29% of registered voters, down from 40% in 2023.

Nigeria's electoral commission, Inec, says it has made efforts to encourage more young people to register ahead of the 2027 general elections.

This includes appointing nine ambassadors from the entertainment industry, spanning film, music and comedy, to reach younger audiences.

But the figures suggest these efforts have yet to make a significant difference.

Dalhatu says he understands the frustration but argues that young Nigerians cannot expect change, if they stay away from the political process.

"Unfortunately, many prefer to just post on social media" instead of getting involved, he says.

Of course being young does not mean you are necessarily the best candidate.

For those who want to participate, there is a formidable obstacle to getting into politics - money.

Dalhatu dreams of becoming president one day, but says he has previously had to abandon campaigns because he could not raise enough funds.

The cost of running for office in Nigeria is notoriously high.

Under the Electoral Act, presidential candidates were allowed to spend up to 5bn naira (£2.8m; $3.7m) on campaigns ahead of the 2023 elections. That spending limit has since been doubled.

The cost of nomination forms alone puts the presidency beyond the reach of most aspiring young Nigerians.

The ruling All Progressive Congress (APC), along with the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and the African Democratic Congress (ADC) have each set their presidential nomination fee at 100m naira ($74,000; £56,000), making it extremely hard for new challengers to emerge.

Since the return to democracy in 1999, only two parties have governed Nigeria - the PDP from 1999 to 2015 and the APC since 2015.

These parties, alongside the ADC, formed last year by politicians who had defected from the other two, have established nationwide network of branches, supporters and campaigners.

Those aspiring candidates without the financial resources to secure nomination forms and compete in the internal party contests of the main parties have little chances of becoming president.

The barriers are also evident in the National Assembly.

Not one of Nigeria's 109 senators is under 40, while only 14 of the 360 members of the House of Representatives fall into that age group.

"I have been in politics for many years and I will tell you that young people in this country lack the resources to become president," says Dalhatu, who is running under Obi's Nigeria Democratic Congress.

Fatima Zahra Umar, a young politician in the APC who has previously tried to run for a seat in the House of Representatives, agrees.

"Young Nigerians are poor. Nigerian politics is cash-intensive, so participation is guided by money," she says, adding that young people are often content with having a bit of influence as a special advisor to a senior politician.

But political analyst Seun Ajayi believes the problems go beyond the financial barriers.

"We have some of the most brilliant young persons in the world, but they are either not interested in politics or feel satisfied when given a small role in government," he says.

"The old men are not going to sit idle and allow us to push them out. We have to fight for the big positions, but at the moment I don't see the zeal."

Umar believes changing attitudes towards young leadership is equally important.

"Culturally, we are not primed to trust or accept the brilliance of a younger person, so it will be very difficult," she says.

"Old men are still holding on to the system."

Some Nigerians took inspiration from the wave of success of young candidates in the recent midterm elections in the US, some of whom have roots in Africa.

"America Has Done It, Can Nigerians Do the Same?" entertainer Charly Boy wrote on X, in a post that was widely shared.

He said the US results served as a warning to Nigerian politicians that no matter how powerful the political machine, voters can change the direction of government.

He called on young people to interrogate candidates about their past promises: "Has life improved? Where are the jobs, security and affordable living?

"Democracy is not a spectator sport, nor is it about sharing rice," he wrote.

articles.title: Meet Mundubai Irappa Davre, the Latur woman who lost 4.5 acres over a Rs 25,000 wedding loan and finally received her land ownership papers back after 30 years
articles.summary: A wedding loan taken in 1995 turned into a three-decade battle over farmland for a woman from Latur, Maharashtra.
articles.body: A wedding loan taken in 1995 turned into a three-decade battle over farmland for a woman from Latur, Maharashtra. After allegedly losing 4.5 acres to a moneylender, Mundubai Irappa Davre has finally reclaimed her land, with the district administration correcting the records and restoring her ownership without asking her to pay the lender.Sometimes, a loan taken to get through one of life's most important moments can turn into a struggle that lasts a lifetime. For Mundubai Irappa Davre, a woman from Kalkuti village in Maharashtra's Latur district, what began as an attempt to arrange her daughter's wedding ended up costing her the land that sustained her family.In 1995, she borrowed Rs 25,000 from a private moneylender and mortgaged 4.5 acres of agricultural land to meet the wedding expenses. She could not have imagined that the arrangement would eventually leave her fighting to reclaim her own land for nearly three decades. Now, after years of uncertainty and repeated attempts to get her property back, Mundubai has finally received her land ownership documents. Her story is not just about recovering farmland but about the long road to justice for someone who had almost lost hope of ever getting her land back.A small loan that came at a huge costMundubai had borrowed Rs 25,000 for her daughter's wedding, keeping her agricultural land as security. According to her account, the moneylender initially took possession of the land on the understanding that agricultural produce would be shared. However, she alleged that the arrangement changed and that the land was eventually transferred in the lender's name using fake witnesses. The land, which was meant to serve as security for a small loan, was no longer under her family's control.The situation became even more difficult when she tried to settle the matter. Mundubai said she offered Rs 2.5 lakh to repay the loan and get her land back. However, the moneylender allegedly refused and demanded Rs 10 lakh, claiming that the amount had grown due to interest. Unable to arrange such a large sum, she was left with little choice but to continue living with the loss of her land.Thirty years of waiting for what was hersFor a family dependent on farming, losing 4.5 acres means losing more than a piece of property. It can mean losing a source of income, security and the ability to plan for the future. Mundubai's prolonged struggle reflects how vulnerable rural families can become when financial distress and land-related disputes collide. The years passed, but the land dispute remained unresolved. Eventually, with financial support from her family, she was able to approach the district administration and seek intervention.The case was examined by local officials. Shelgaon Circle Officer Mahesh Hipparge told PTI that a sale deed had allegedly been executed in 1995 against the Rs 25,000 loan. Following an order from Latur Collector Bharat Bastwad and approval from the tehsildar, the administration corrected the land records and restored Mundubai's name as the owner. This administrative intervention became the turning point in a dispute that had continued for nearly 30 years.The papers that finally brought her home her landOn November 19, during Maharashtra Governor Jishnu Dev Varma's visit to Latur, Mundubai was handed her land documents, including the 7/12 extract, commonly known as the Satbara. It is an important revenue record in Maharashtra that contains details of land ownership and agricultural holdings. The document was more than a piece of official paperwork. It represented the restoration of her ownership after decades of uncertainty. According to reports, she got the land back without having to pay the moneylender anything.Mundubai expressed gratitude to the district collector, Superintendent of Police Amol Tambe, and the local tehsildar for helping her reclaim the property. The intervention brought an end to a long and exhausting battle over land that her family had originally mortgaged to arrange a wedding.Her story is a reminder that behind land records, loan agreements and revenue documents are people whose lives can be shaped by a single financial decision. For Mundubai, the Rs 25,000 borrowed nearly three decades ago had come to represent years of struggle. Getting her name back on the land records has finally given her something she had been fighting for all along: her rightful place on her own land.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: California train burglars carefully executed heists for ‘staggering’ $22m haul
articles.summary: US justice department brings charges against group after at least 36 trains burglarized for shoes and tools
articles.body:
Fourteen people in southern California have been accused of burglarizing more than $22m worth of goods from moving freight trains, in a plot reminiscent of the US old west, when outlaws and bandits wreaked havoc on the nascent railroad industry.

The justice department has brought railroad theft charges against the group for raiding at least 36 trains and selling thousands of stolen Nike sneakers, among other products, on the black market.

"The scale of the theft is staggering," first assistant US attorney Bill Essayli said.

Nathan Daniel Angel, 21, was the alleged ringleader for the so-called "Los Trenes" ("the trains") scheme, which spanned 2024 through 2026. Court documents did not list an attorney for Angel or the other charged individuals.

Angel's associates, including his father and two uncles, stowed away on moving freight trains, according to a grand jury indictment.

With some of the men on board serving as lookouts, the others would slash the train's air hose, causing a sudden loss of air pressure and forcing an emergency stop of the entire vehicle. The maneuver is perilous given the risks of derailment.

Once the train was disabled, the rest of the Los Trenes crew would swoop in to load up the stolen goods and stash the loot at houses across southern California, prosecutors say.

Angel posed for a selfie, where he threw up the peace sign, in front of several boxes containing Nike merchandise, in a February 2024 photograph, attached to court documents.

The next burglary would come months later.

In October 2024, Donta Hedgeman, 27, sawed through the lock of a container on a moving Nike train, according to video evidence.

The heists ramped up in 2025, even as signs emerged that law enforcement was catching on to the alleged thefts.

An unidentified "co-conspirator" texted 23-year-old Carlos Luis Fernando Martinez on 17 April 2025 to say he had been arrested for receiving stolen property.

"They want me to tell them who did I get them from and who had the other pairs," the person wrote.

Martinez responded, instructing the person to contact him over Signal, an app with encrypted messaging.

Twelve days later, the crew made off with 1,170 tools and 17,000 parts from Milwaukee Tool.

Police officers appeared to sniff around an unnamed company, which purchased a slew of stolen products from the crew in the fall of 2025.

A different "co-conspirator" speculated on their fate. "Good luck with them wires/if they go deep in the case/You're cooked," they wrote to Martinez.

Then, on 16 January 2026, Angel and 25-year-old Fredy Marquina referenced a partner being intercepted by police: "They just got Jorge for buying and receiving/stolen property."

Once again, faced with the mounting risk of being caught, the men proceeded with further heists in the summer of 2026.

In July 2026, Angel Sanchez, 24, shared an AI-generated image that appeared to glamorize their robbery spree.

Masked men tossed Nike sneakers off a Burlington Northern Santa Fe Railway (BNSR) train into luxury cars inscribed with the words "Los Trenes".

In the image, a helicopter circled above, shining a searchlight.

If convicted of the conspiracy charge, the men face at least five years in prison. The theft of interstate railroad charge has a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison.

A conviction for violence against railroad carriers would carry the most severe punishment with a possibility of life in prison.

Prosecutors described this week's sweeping indictment as the culmination of a 14-month-long investigation.

"We are determined to protect this vital supply chain and ensure that goods reach their intended destinations, not the black market," said Nathan Hochman, the Los Angeles county district attorney.

articles.title: Trump asks federal contractors to withhold 'privileged information' from Congress; Democrats cry foul
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has directed federal contractors and subcontractors to consult his administration before responding to inquiries from Congress
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has directed federal contractors and subcontractors to consult his administration before responding to inquiries from Congress and withhold information that the White House considers protected by executive privilege.Under a new executive order issued late Friday, companies must coordinate with the White House and federal agencies on “appropriate responses” to congressional requests, with non-compliance potentially resulting in the termination of their government contracts and suspension from future federal work.The order applies to tens of thousands of businesses working as federal contractors and subcontractors. It marks the Trump administration's latest move to restrict how information is shared with Congress ahead of January, when Democrats are set to take control of the legislature and are expected to intensify scrutiny of the administration, AP reported.Democrats have identified federal contracts as a major target for investigations, pointing to the flow of government funds to companies linked to Trump's family, particularly through the Pentagon.White House tightens control over congressional inquiriesThe executive order follows steps by White House officials to exercise greater control over how government agencies and officials handle congressional requests.Trump's counsel, Will Scharf, told federal agencies on Monday that they must obtain approval from his office and the White House's Office of Legislative Affairs before agreeing to appear before Congress, AP reported.In a recent letter to representative Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, Scharf also suggested that some congressional investigations could amount to “blatant criminality”.Garcia had sent letters this week asking members of Trump's family and senior administration officials to preserve documents. Scharf sought to dismiss the requests, arguing that Democrats were not yet in the congressional majority and therefore could not compel compliance.Reacting to the executive order on Saturday, Garcia described it as part of the administration's “blatant attack on Congress’ constitutional right to conduct oversight”. He added that despite efforts to obstruct investigations, “we're just getting started.”Representative Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat leading investigations on the House Judiciary Committee, also criticised the order, calling it “totally unprecedented and blatantly unlawful”. He said government contractors had a “duty and a right to speak truthfully when Congress calls”.White House cites executive privilegeIn a fact sheet, the White House described the new requirements as a measure to protect executive privilege from congressional overreach. It accused some congressional leaders of attempting to intrude on executive branch privileges by “harassing private companies that contract with the federal government”.Presidents from both parties have historically invoked executive privilege to resist congressional inquiries. However, such claims can lead to prolonged legal disputes over whether the protection applies in specific cases.Executive privilege allows a president to withhold certain information from Congress, courts and the public to preserve the confidentiality of White House deliberations, although the protection is not absolute.You use AI every day. articles.title: Sacred relics of Lord Buddha to be displayed at Sarnath from Nov 22-24
articles.summary: Sacred relics of Lord Buddha to be displayed at Sarnath’s Mulagandha Kuti Vihar Nov 22-24, marking the shrine’s 95th anniversary.
articles.body: Varanasi: Following Sarnath’s Unesco World Heritage recognition earlier this year, the sacred relics of Lord Buddha will be displayed for public veneration at Mulagandha Kuti Vihar from Nov 22 to 24.The three-day exposition will coincide with the 95th anniversary commemoration of the shrine at Sarnath, the sacred site where Lord Buddha delivered his first sermon, known as the Dharmachakra Pravartana.The ceremony is being organised by the Maha Bodhi Society of India, Sarnath Centre, in collaboration with the Venerable Vietnamese Sangha and devotees from Hanoi. Their support has made the exposition of the relics possible.During the event, the relics enshrined beneath the golden Buddha statue inside Mulagandha Kuti Vihar will be ceremonially brought out for devotees to pay their respects.Monks, pilgrims and Buddhist followers from India, Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia, Nepal, Japan and several other countries are expected to attend.Tourism and culture minister Jaiveer Singh said Sarnath holds a special place on India’s spiritual map. He said it was a matter of pride for Uttar Pradesh that the ancient Buddhist site of Sarnath in Varanasi was inscribed on the Unesco World Heritage List on July 25, making it India’s 45th and Uttar Pradesh’s fourth World Heritage Site.He said the recognition had given Sarnath greater global prominence and strengthened its position as a major destination for Buddhist devotees, scholars and tourists.According to the minister, Buddhist sites in Uttar Pradesh received nearly 28 lakh visitors in 2016. By 2025, the number had increased to more than 82 lakh, registering a rise of nearly 200%. In the first half of 2026 alone, Sarnath attracted close to three lakh visitors, reflecting its growing importance in spiritual and cultural tourism.Mulagandha Kuti Vihar houses two important relics of Lord Buddha, discovered at separate archaeological sites.The first relic was excavated in 1929 by AH Longhurst, Superintendent of the Archaeological Survey of India’s Southern Circle, from a large stupa at Nagarjunakonda in present-day Andhra Pradesh. An inscription at the site identifies the stupa as the Mahachetiya of Gautama Buddha.The second relic was discovered by Sir John Marshall in 1913–14 in a small chapel near the Dharmarajika Stupa at ancient Taxila, in present-day Pakistan. It was found along with a silver scroll bearing an inscription referring to the relics of the Buddha.Both relics were presented to the Maha Bodhi Society in 1931 and 1932 by the then Viceroy and Governor General of India, the Earl of Willingdon, for enshrinement at Sarnath. They are now preserved in specially prepared silver caskets inside Mulagandha Kuti Vihar.The relics are displayed only twice a year, on Buddha Purnima and Kartika Purnima, making the upcoming exposition a significant occasion for the Buddhist community.After the ceremony concludes on Nov 24, the relics will be respectfully re-enshrined beneath the golden statue of Lord Buddha.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Varanasi | Silver Rate in Varanasi | Bank Holidays in Varanasi | Public Holidays in Varanasi | Varanasi AQI | Weather in Varanasi | Petrol Price in Varanasi | Diesel Price in Varanasi | CNG Price in Varanasi | LPG Price in VaranasiStay updated with the latest Varanasi news.
